slides.heading: Minimum Waiting Time
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Easy · Greedy Algorithms
slides.narration: Let's solve Minimum Waiting Time, an easy greedy algorithms problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Short queries should run first, because each query's duration is waited on by everyone after it.
slides.narration: Short queries should run first, because each query's duration is waited on by everyone after it.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Brute force: try every order → n! permutations
Greedy: shortest first is optimal → O(n log n)
Each duration counts once per query behind it
slides.narration: Trying every execution order is factorial. Exchange argument: if a longer query runs before a shorter one, swapping them reduces total waiting. So shortest first is optimal, and sorting costs n log n.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 2. Each duration is waited on by the queries remaining after it
slides.narration: Step by step. First, sort durations ascending. Second, each duration is waited on by the queries remaining after it. Third, add duration times queries left. Fourth, return the total.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Sort: [3, 2, 1, 2, 6] → [1, 2, 2, 3, 6]
slides.narration: Take the queries three, two, one, two, six. Sorted, they become one, two, two, three, six.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 1 s is waited on by 4 queries → total 4
slides.narration: Query 0 takes 1 seconds, and the 4 queries after it all wait for it, adding 4. The total is now 4.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 2 s is waited on by 3 queries → total 10
slides.narration: Query 1 takes 2 seconds, and the 3 queries after it all wait for it, adding 6. The total is now 10.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 3 s is waited on by 1 queries → total 17
slides.narration: Query 3 takes 3 seconds, and the 1 queries after it all wait for it, adding 3. The total is now 17.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 6 s is waited on by 0 queries → total 17
slides.narration: Query 4 takes 6 seconds, and the 0 queries after it all wait for it, adding 0. The total is now 17.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We sort the array, then for each index multiply the duration by the number of queries left after it and add it to the total.

slides.heading: Complexity
bullets: Time: queries with durations run one at a time; choose an order minimising the total time all queries spend waiting. Shortest-first is optimal. Time: O(n log n)
slides.narration: Time is queries with durations run one at a time; choose an order minimising the total time all queries spend waiting. Shortest-first is optimal. Time is O of n log n. Space is constant.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: The last query adds 0 (nobody waits for it)
Sorting in place mutates input (mention it)
slides.narration: The last query contributes nothing. Sorting in place mutates the input, which you should mention. Use a long if totals can be large.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: Follow-up: weighted queries (Smith's rule: sort by time/weight)
slides.narration: Prove the greedy with an exchange argument. A follow-up adds weights, where you sort by duration divided by weight.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Short queries should run first, because each query's duration is waited on by everyone after it.
Complexity: queries with durations run one at a time; choose an order minimising the total time all queries spend waiting. Shortest-first is optimal. Time: O(n log n)
